segs.p: Atthi, bhikkhave, puggalo ajjhupekkhitabbo na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo na payirupāsitabbo.
segs.e: There is an individual you should regard with equanimity, and you shouldn’t associate with, accompany, or attend them.

segs.p: Atthi, bhikkhave, puggalo sevitabbo bhajitabbo payirupāsitabbo.
segs.e: There is an individual you should associate with, accompany, and attend.

segs.p: Katamo ca, bhikkhave, puggalo jigucchitabbo na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo na payirupāsitabbo?
segs.e: Who is the individual you should be disgusted by, and not associate with, accompany, or attend?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo dussīlo hoti pāpadhammo asuci saṅkassarasamācāro paṭicchannakammanto, assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiñño, abrahmacārī brahmacāripaṭiñño, antopūti avassuto kasambujāto.
segs.e: It’s an individual who is unethical, of bad qualities, filthy, with suspicious behavior, underhand, no true ascetic or spiritual practitioner—though claiming to be one—rotten inside, festering, and depraved.

segs.p: Evarūpo, bhikkhave, puggalo jigucchitabbo na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo na payirupāsitabbo.
segs.e: You should be disgusted by such an individual, and you shouldn’t associate with, accompany, or attend them.
Why is that?

segs.p: Kiñcāpi, bhikkhave, evarūpassa puggalassa na diṭṭhānugatiṁ āpajjati, atha kho naṁ pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati:
segs.e: Even if you don’t follow the example of such an individual, you still get a bad reputation:
‘That individual has bad friends, companions, and associates.’

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ahi gūthagato kiñcāpi na daṁsati, atha kho naṁ makkheti;
segs.e: They’re like a snake that’s been living in a pile of dung. Even if it doesn’t bite, it’ll still rub off on you.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, kiñcāpi evarūpassa puggalassa na diṭṭhānugatiṁ āpajjati, atha kho naṁ pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati:
segs.e: In the same way, even if you don’t follow the example of such an individual, you still get a bad reputation:
‘That individual has bad friends, companions, and associates.’

segs.p: Tasmā evarūpo puggalo jigucchitabbo na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo na payirupāsitabbo.
segs.e: That’s why you should be disgusted by such an individual, and you shouldn’t associate with, accompany, or attend them.

segs.p: Katamo ca, bhikkhave, puggalo ajjhupekkhitabbo na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo na payirupāsitabbo?
segs.e: Who is the individual you should regard with equanimity, and not associate with, accompany, or attend?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo kodhano hoti upāyāsabahulo,
segs.e: It’s an individual who is irritable and bad-tempered.

segs.p: appampi vutto samāno abhisajjati kuppati byāpajjati patitthīyati, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti.
segs.e: Even when lightly criticized they lose their temper, becoming annoyed, hostile, and hard-hearted, and they display annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, duṭṭhāruko kaṭṭhena vā kaṭhalāya vā ghaṭṭito bhiyyoso mattāya āsavaṁ deti;
segs.e: They’re like a festering sore, which, when you hit it with a stick or a stone, discharges even more.
In the same way, someone is irritable and bad-tempered.

segs.p: seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, tindukālātaṁ kaṭṭhena vā kaṭhalāya vā ghaṭṭitaṁ bhiyyoso mattāya cicciṭāyati ciṭiciṭāyati;
segs.e: They’re like a firebrand of pale-moon ebony, which, when you hit it with a stick or a stone, sizzles and crackles even more.
In the same way, someone is irritable and bad-tempered.

segs.p: seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gūthakūpo kaṭṭhena vā kaṭhalāya vā ghaṭṭito bhiyyoso mattāya duggandho hoti;
segs.e: They’re like a sewer, which, when you stir it with a stick or a stone, stinks even more.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco puggalo kodhano hoti upāyāsabahulo,
segs.e: In the same way, an individual is irritable and bad-tempered.

segs.p: appampi vutto samāno abhisajjati kuppati byāpajjati patitthīyati, kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukaroti.
segs.e: Even when lightly criticized they lose their temper, becoming annoyed, hostile, and hard-hearted, and they display annoyance, hate, and bitterness.

segs.p: Evarūpo, bhikkhave, puggalo ajjhupekkhitabbo na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo na payirupāsitabbo.
segs.e: You should regard such an individual with equanimity, and you shouldn’t associate with, accompany, or attend them.
Why is that?

segs.p: Akkoseyyapi maṁ paribhāseyyapi maṁ anatthampi maṁ kareyyāti.
segs.e: Thinking, ‘They might abuse or insult me, or do me harm.’

segs.p: Tasmā evarūpo puggalo ajjhupekkhitabbo na sevitabbo na bhajitabbo na payirupāsitabbo.
segs.e: That’s why you should regard such an individual with equanimity, and you shouldn’t associate with, accompany, or attend them.

segs.p: Katamo ca, bhikkhave, puggalo sevitabbo bhajitabbo payirupāsitabbo?
segs.e: Who is the individual you should associate with, accompany, and attend?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo sīlavā hoti kalyāṇadhammo.
segs.e: It’s an individual who is ethical, of good character.

segs.p: Evarūpo, bhikkhave, puggalo sevitabbo bhajitabbo payirupāsitabbo.
segs.e: You should associate with, accompany, and attend such an individual.
Why is that?

segs.p: Kiñcāpi, bhikkhave, evarūpassa puggalassa na diṭṭhānugatiṁ āpajjati, atha kho naṁ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchati:
segs.e: Even if you don’t follow the example of such an individual, you still get a good reputation:
‘That individual has good friends, companions, and associates.’

segs.p: Tasmā evarūpo puggalo sevitabbo bhajitabbo payirupāsitabbo.
segs.e: That’s why you should associate with, accompany, and attend such an individual.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, tayo puggalā santo saṁvijjamānā lokasminti.
segs.e: These are the three individuals found in the world.
A man who associates with an inferior goes downhill,
but associating with an equal, you’ll never decline;
following the best, you’ll quickly rise up,
so you should keep company <j>with people better than you.”
Numbered Discourses 3.28
3. Individuals
Speech like Dung
“These three individuals are found in the world.
What three?
One with speech like dung, one with speech like flowers, and one with speech like honey.
And who has speech like dung?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo sabhaggato vā parisaggato vā ñātimajjhagato vā pūgamajjhagato vā rājakulamajjhagato vā abhinīto sakkhipuṭṭho: ‘ehambho purisa, yaṁ jānāsi taṁ vadehī’ti. So ajānaṁ vā āha: ‘jānāmī’ti, jānaṁ vā āha: ‘na jānāmī’ti, apassaṁ vā āha: ‘passāmī’ti, passaṁ vā āha: ‘na passāmī’ti; iti attahetu vā parahetu vā āmisakiñcikkhahetu vā sampajānamusā bhāsitā hoti.
segs.e: It’s an individual who is summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my man, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ So they deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.
This is called an individual with speech like dung.
And who has speech like flowers?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo sabhaggato vā parisaggato vā ñātimajjhagato vā pūgamajjhagato vā rājakulamajjhagato vā abhinīto sakkhipuṭṭho: ‘ehambho purisa, yaṁ pajānāsi taṁ vadehī’ti, so ajānaṁ vā āha: ‘na jānāmī’ti, jānaṁ vā āha: ‘jānāmī’ti, apassaṁ vā āha: ‘na passāmī’ti, passaṁ vā āha: ‘passāmī’ti; iti attahetu vā parahetu vā āmisakiñcikkhahetu vā na sampajānamusā bhāsitā hoti.
segs.e: It’s an individual who is summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: ‘Please, my man, say what you know.’ Not knowing, they say ‘I don’t know.’ Knowing, they say ‘I know.’ Not seeing, they say ‘I don’t see.’ And seeing, they say ‘I see.’ So they don’t deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason.
This is called an individual with speech like flowers.
And who has speech like honey?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo pharusaṁ vācaṁ pahāya pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti;
segs.e: It’s an individual who gives up harsh speech.

segs.p: yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā pemanīyā hadayaṅgamā porī bahujanakantā bahujanamanāpā tathārūpiṁ vācaṁ bhāsitā hoti.
segs.e: They speak in a way that’s mellow, pleasing to the ear, endearing, going to the heart, polite, and likable and agreeable to the people.
This is called an individual with speech like honey.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, tayo puggalā santo saṁvijjamānā lokasmin”ti.
segs.e: These are the three individuals found in the world.”
Numbered Discourses 3.29
3. Individuals
Blind
“These three individuals are found in the world.
What three?
The blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed.
Who is the blind individual?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekaccassa puggalassa tathārūpaṁ cakkhu na hoti yathārūpena cakkhunā anadhigataṁ vā bhogaṁ adhigaccheyya adhigataṁ vā bhogaṁ phātiṁ kareyya;
segs.e: It’s someone who doesn’t have the kind of vision that’s needed to acquire more wealth or to increase the wealth they’ve already acquired.

segs.p: tathārūpampissa cakkhu na hoti yathārūpena cakkhunā kusalākusale dhamme jāneyya, sāvajjānavajje dhamme jāneyya, hīnappaṇīte dhamme jāneyya, kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhamme jāneyya.
segs.e: Nor do they have the kind of vision that’s needed to know the difference between qualities that are skillful and unskillful, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior, and those with a portion of dark or bright.
This is called a blind individual.
Who is the individual with one eye?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekaccassa puggalassa tathārūpaṁ cakkhu hoti yathārūpena cakkhunā anadhigataṁ vā bhogaṁ adhigaccheyya adhigataṁ vā bhogaṁ phātiṁ kareyya;
segs.e: It’s someone who has the kind of vision that’s needed to acquire more wealth and to increase the wealth they’ve already acquired.

segs.p: tathārūpaṁ panassa cakkhu na hoti yathārūpena cakkhunā kusalākusale dhamme jāneyya, sāvajjānavajje dhamme jāneyya, hīnappaṇīte dhamme jāneyya, kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhamme jāneyya.
segs.e: But they don’t have the kind of vision that’s needed to know the difference between qualities that are skillful and unskillful, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior, and those with a portion of dark or bright.
This is called a one-eyed individual.
Who is the individual with two eyes?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekaccassa puggalassa tathārūpaṁ cakkhu hoti yathārūpena cakkhunā anadhigataṁ vā bhogaṁ adhigaccheyya, adhigataṁ vā bhogaṁ phātiṁ kareyya;
segs.e: It’s someone who has the kind of vision that’s needed to acquire more wealth and to increase the wealth they’ve already acquired.

segs.p: tathārūpampissa cakkhu hoti yathārūpena cakkhunā kusalākusale dhamme jāneyya;
segs.e: And they have the kind of vision that’s needed to know the difference between skillful and unskillful, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior, or qualities on the side of dark and bright.

segs.p: sāvajjānavajje dhamme jāneyya, hīnappaṇīte dhamme jāneyya, kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhamme jāneyya.

segs.e: This is called a two-eyed individual.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, tayo puggalā santo saṁvijjamānā lokasminti.
segs.e: These are the three individuals found in the world.
Neither suitable wealth,
nor merit do they make.
They hold a losing hand on both counts,
those who are blind, with ruined eyes.
And now the one-eyed
individual is explained.
By methods good and bad,
that devious person seeks wealth.
Both by fraudulent, thieving deeds,
and also by lies,
the young man’s skilled at piling up money,
and enjoying sensual pleasures.
From here they go to hell—
the one-eyed person is ruined.
And now the two-eyed is explained,
the best individual.
Their wealth is earned legitimately,
money acquired by their own hard work.
They give with best of intentions,
that peaceful-hearted man.
They go to a good place,
where there is no sorrow.
The blind and the one-eyed,
you should avoid from afar.
But you should keep the two-eyed close,
the best individual.”
Numbered Discourses 3.30
3. Individuals
Upside-down
“These three individuals are found in the world.
What three?

segs.p: Avakujjapañño puggalo, ucchaṅgapañño puggalo, puthupañño puggalo.
segs.e: One with upside-down wisdom, one with wisdom on their lap, and one with widespread wisdom.
And who is the individual with upside-down wisdom?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo ārāmaṁ gantā hoti abhikkhaṇaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ santike dhammassavanāya.
segs.e: It’s an individual who often goes to the monastery to hear the teaching in the presence of the mendicants.

segs.p: Tassa bhikkhū dhammaṁ desenti ādikalyāṇaṁ majjhekalyāṇaṁ pariyosānakalyāṇaṁ sātthaṁ sabyañjanaṁ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṁ parisuddhaṁ brahmacariyaṁ pakāsenti.
segs.e: The mendicants teach them Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And they reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

segs.p: So tasmiṁ āsane nisinno tassā kathāya neva ādiṁ manasi karoti, na majjhaṁ manasi karoti, na pariyosānaṁ manasi karoti;
segs.e: But even while sitting there, that person doesn’t apply the mind to the beginning, middle, or end of the discussion.

segs.p: vuṭṭhitopi tamhā āsanā tassā kathāya neva ādiṁ manasi karoti, na majjhaṁ manasi karoti, na pariyosānaṁ manasi karoti.
segs.e: And when they rise from their seat, they don’t apply the mind to the beginning, middle, or end of the discussion.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kumbho nikujjo tatra udakaṁ āsittaṁ vivaṭṭati, no saṇṭhāti;
segs.e: It’s like when a pot full of water is tipped over, so the water drains out and doesn’t stay.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco puggalo ārāmaṁ gantā hoti abhikkhaṇaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ santike dhammassavanāya.
segs.e: In the same way, an individual often goes to the monastery to hear the teaching in the presence of the mendicants.

segs.p: Tassa bhikkhū dhammaṁ desenti ādikalyāṇaṁ majjhekalyāṇaṁ pariyosānakalyāṇaṁ sātthaṁ sabyañjanaṁ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṁ parisuddhaṁ brahmacariyaṁ pakāsenti.
segs.e: The mendicants teach them Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And they reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

segs.p: So tasmiṁ āsane nisinno tassā kathāya neva ādiṁ manasi karoti, na majjhaṁ manasi karoti, na pariyosānaṁ manasi karoti;
segs.e: But even while sitting there, that person doesn’t apply the mind to the discussion in the beginning, middle, or end.

segs.p: vuṭṭhitopi tamhā āsanā tassā kathāya neva ādiṁ manasi karoti, na majjhaṁ manasi karoti, na pariyosānaṁ manasi karoti.
segs.e: And when they rise from their seat, they don’t apply the mind to the beginning, middle, or end of the discussion.
This is called an individual with upside-down wisdom.
And who is the individual with wisdom on their lap?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo ārāmaṁ gantā hoti abhikkhaṇaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ santike dhammassavanāya.
segs.e: It’s an individual who often goes to the monastery to hear the teaching in the presence of the mendicants.

segs.p: Tassa bhikkhū dhammaṁ desenti ādikalyāṇaṁ majjhekalyāṇaṁ pariyosānakalyāṇaṁ sātthaṁ sabyañjanaṁ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṁ parisuddhaṁ brahmacariyaṁ pakāsenti.
segs.e: The mendicants teach them Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And they reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

segs.p: So tasmiṁ āsane nisinno tassā kathāya ādimpi manasi karoti, majjhampi manasi karoti, pariyosānampi manasi karoti;
segs.e: While sitting there, that person applies the mind to the discussion in the beginning, middle, and end.

segs.p: vuṭṭhito ca kho tamhā āsanā tassā kathāya neva ādiṁ manasi karoti, na majjhaṁ manasi karoti, na pariyosānaṁ manasi karoti.
segs.e: But when they rise from their seat, they don’t apply the mind to the beginning, middle, or end of the discussion.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, purisassa ucchaṅge nānākhajjakāni ākiṇṇāni—
segs.e: It’s like a person who has different kinds of food crammed on their lap—
such as sesame, rice, sweets, or jujube—

segs.p: So tamhā āsanā vuṭṭhahanto satisammosā pakireyya.
segs.e: so that if they rise from the seat without mindfulness, everything gets scattered.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco puggalo ārāmaṁ gantā hoti abhikkhaṇaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ santike dhammassavanāya.
segs.e: In the same way, an individual often goes to the monastery to hear the teaching in the presence of the mendicants.

segs.p: Tassa bhikkhū dhammaṁ desenti ādikalyāṇaṁ majjhekalyāṇaṁ pariyosānakalyāṇaṁ sātthaṁ sabyañjanaṁ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṁ parisuddhaṁ brahmacariyaṁ pakāsenti.
segs.e: The mendicants teach them Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And they reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

segs.p: So tasmiṁ āsane nisinno tassā kathāya ādimpi manasi karoti, majjhampi manasi karoti, pariyosānampi manasi karoti;
segs.e: While sitting there, that person applies the mind to the discussion in the beginning, middle, and end.

segs.p: vuṭṭhito ca kho tamhā āsanā tassā kathāya neva ādiṁ manasi karoti, na majjhaṁ manasi karoti, na pariyosānaṁ manasi karoti.
segs.e: But when they rise from their seat, they don’t apply the mind to the beginning, middle, or end of the discussion.
This is called an individual with wisdom on their lap.
And who is the individual with widespread wisdom?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco puggalo ārāmaṁ gantā hoti abhikkhaṇaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ santike dhammassavanāya.
segs.e: It’s an individual who often goes to the monastery to hear the teaching in the presence of the mendicants.

segs.p: Tassa bhikkhū dhammaṁ desenti ādikalyāṇaṁ majjhekalyāṇaṁ pariyosānakalyāṇaṁ sātthaṁ sabyañjanaṁ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṁ parisuddhaṁ brahmacariyaṁ pakāsenti.
segs.e: The mendicants teach them Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And they reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

segs.p: So tasmiṁ āsane nisinno tassā kathāya ādimpi manasi karoti, majjhampi manasi karoti, pariyosānampi manasi karoti;
segs.e: While sitting there, they apply the mind to the discussion in the beginning, middle, and end.

segs.p: vuṭṭhitopi tamhā āsanā tassā kathāya ādimpi manasi karoti, majjhampi manasi karoti, pariyosānampi manasi karoti.
segs.e: And when they rise from their seat, they continue to apply the mind to the beginning, middle, or end of the discussion.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kumbho ukkujjo tatra udakaṁ āsittaṁ saṇṭhāti no vivaṭṭati;
segs.e: It’s like when a pot full of water is set straight, so the water stays and doesn’t drain out.

segs.p: evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco puggalo ārāmaṁ gantā hoti abhikkhaṇaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ santike dhammassavanāya.
segs.e: In the same way, an individual often goes to the monastery to hear the teaching in the presence of the mendicants.

segs.p: Tassa bhikkhū dhammaṁ desenti ādikalyāṇaṁ majjhekalyāṇaṁ pariyosānakalyāṇaṁ sātthaṁ sabyañjanaṁ, kevalaparipuṇṇaṁ parisuddhaṁ brahmacariyaṁ pakāsenti.
segs.e: The mendicants teach them Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And they reveal a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure.

segs.p: So tasmiṁ āsane nisinno tassā kathāya ādimpi manasi karoti, majjhampi manasi karoti, pariyosānampi manasi karoti;
segs.e: While sitting there, they apply the mind to the discussion in the beginning, middle, and end.

segs.p: vuṭṭhitopi tamhā āsanā tassā kathāya ādimpi manasi karoti, majjhampi manasi karoti, pariyosānampi manasi karoti.
segs.e: And when they rise from their seat, they continue to apply the mind to the beginning, middle, or end of the discussion.
This is called an individual with widespread wisdom.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, tayo puggalā santo saṁvijjamānā lokasminti.
segs.e: These are the three individuals found in the world.
A person with upside-down wisdom,
is a simpleton and cannot see,
and even if they frequently
go into the mendicants’ presence,
such a person can’t learn
the beginning, middle, or end
of the discussion,
for their wisdom is lacking.
the individual with wisdom on their lap
is better than that, it’s said;
but even if they frequently
go into the mendicants’ presence,
such a person can only learn
the beginning, middle, and end
while sitting in that seat;
but they’ve only grasped the phrasing,
for when they rise their understanding fails,
and what they’ve learned is lost.
The person with widespread wisdom
is better than that, it’s said;
and if they, too, frequently
go into the mendicants’ presence,
one such can learn
the beginning, middle, and end
while sitting in that seat;
and when they’ve grasped the phrasing,
they remember it with the best of intentions.
That peaceful-hearted man,
practicing in line with the teaching,
would make an end of suffering.”
Numbered Discourses 3.31
4. Messengers of the Gods
With Divinity

segs.p: “Sabrahmakāni, bhikkhave, tāni kulāni yesaṁ puttānaṁ mātāpitaro ajjhāgāre pūjitā honti.
segs.e: “Mendicants, a family where the children honor their parents in their home is said to live with divinity.

segs.p: Sapubbācariyakāni, bhikkhave, tāni kulāni yesaṁ puttānaṁ mātāpitaro ajjhāgāre pūjitā honti.
segs.e: A family where the children honor their parents in their home is said to live with the first tutors.

segs.p: Sāhuneyyāni, bhikkhave, tāni kulāni yesaṁ puttānaṁ mātāpitaro ajjhāgāre pūjitā honti.
segs.e: A family where the children honor their parents in their home is said to live with those worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods.
‘Divinity’ is a term for your parents.
‘First tutors’ is a term for your parents.
‘Worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods’ is a term for your parents.
Why is that?

segs.p: Bahukārā, bhikkhave, mātāpitaro puttānaṁ, āpādakā posakā, imassa lokassa dassetāroti.
segs.e: Parents are very helpful to their children, they raise them, nurture them, and show them the world.
Parents are said to be ‘divinity’
and ‘first tutors’, it’s said.
They’re worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods <j>from their children,
for they love their offspring.
Therefore an astute person
would revere them and honor them
with food and drink,
clothes and bedding,
anointing and bathing,
and by washing their feet.
Because they look after
their parents like this,
in this life they’re praised by the astute,
and they depart to rejoice in heaven.”
Numbered Discourses 3.32
4. Messengers of the Gods
With Ānanda

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Ānanda went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him:

segs.p: “Siyā nu kho, bhante, bhikkhuno tathārūpo samādhipaṭilābho yathā imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā nāssu, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā nāssu;
segs.e: “Could it be, sir, that a mendicant might gain a state of immersion such that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body; and no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for externally for all signs;

segs.p: yañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja viharato ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na honti tañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja vihareyyā”ti?
segs.e: and that they’d live having attained the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit are no more?”

segs.p: “Siyā, ānanda, bhikkhuno tathārūpo samādhipaṭilābho yathā imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā nāssu, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā nāssu;
segs.e: “It could be, Ānanda, that a mendicant gains a state of immersion such that they have no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body; and no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for externally for all signs;

segs.p: yañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja viharato ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na honti tañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja vihareyyā”ti.
segs.e: and that they’d live having attained the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit are no more.”

segs.p: “Yathā kathaṁ pana, bhante, siyā bhikkhuno tathārūpo samādhipaṭilābho yathā imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā nāssu, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā nāssu;
segs.e: “But how could this be, sir?”

segs.p: yañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja viharato ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na honti tañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja vihareyyā”ti?

segs.e: “Ānanda, it’s when a mendicant thinks:

segs.p: ‘etaṁ santaṁ etaṁ paṇītaṁ yadidaṁ sabbasaṅkhārasamatho sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbānan’ti.
segs.e: ‘This is peaceful; this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all activities, the letting go of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment.’

segs.p: Evaṁ kho, ānanda, siyā bhikkhuno tathārūpo samādhipaṭilābho yathā imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā nāssu, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā nāssu;
segs.e: That’s how, Ānanda, a mendicant might gain a state of immersion such that there’s no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body; and no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for externally for all signs;

segs.p: yañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja viharato ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na honti tañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja vihareyyāti.
segs.e: and that they’d live having achieved the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit are no more.

segs.p: Idañca pana metaṁ, ānanda, sandhāya bhāsitaṁ pārāyane puṇṇakapañhe:
segs.e: And Ānanda, this is what I was referring to in ‘The Way to the Far Shore’, in ‘The Questions of Puṇṇaka’ when I said:
‘Having appraised the world high and low,
there is nothing in the world that disturbs them.
Peaceful, unclouded, untroubled, <j>with no need for hope—
they’ve crossed over rebirth and old age, I declare.’”
Numbered Discourses 3.33
4. Messengers of the Gods
With Sāriputta

segs.p: Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinnaṁ kho āyasmantaṁ sāriputtaṁ bhagavā etadavoca:
segs.e: Then Venerable Sāriputta went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to him,
“Maybe I’ll teach Dhamma in brief,

segs.p: vitthārenapi kho ahaṁ, sāriputta, dhammaṁ deseyyaṁ;
segs.e: maybe in detail,

segs.p: saṅkhittavitthārenapi kho ahaṁ, sāriputta, dhammaṁ deseyyaṁ;
segs.e: maybe both in brief and in detail.
But it’s hard to find anyone who understands.”
“Now is the time, Blessed One! Now is the time, Holy One!

segs.p: yaṁ bhagavā saṅkhittenapi dhammaṁ deseyya, vitthārenapi dhammaṁ deseyya, saṅkhittavitthārenapi dhammaṁ deseyya.
segs.e: Let the Buddha teach Dhamma in brief, in detail, and both in brief and in detail.
There will be those who understand the teaching!”
“So, Sāriputta, you should train like this:

segs.p: ‘imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na bhavissanti, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na bhavissanti, yañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja viharato ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na honti tañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja viharissāmā’ti.
segs.e: ‘There’ll be no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body; and no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit externally for all signs; and we’ll live having achieved the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit are no more.’
That’s how you should train.

segs.p: Yato ca kho, sāriputta, bhikkhuno imasmiñca saviññāṇake kāye ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na honti, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittesu ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na honti, yañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja viharato ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayā na honti tañca cetovimuttiṁ paññāvimuttiṁ upasampajja viharati;
segs.e: When a mendicant has no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit for this conscious body; and no I-making, mine-making, or underlying tendency to conceit externally for all signs; and they live having attained the freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit are no more—
they’re called

segs.p: ‘bhikkhu acchecchi taṇhaṁ, vivattayi saṁyojanaṁ, sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassa’.
segs.e: a mendicant who has cut off craving, cast off the fetters, and by rightly comprehending conceit has made an end of suffering.

segs.p: Idañca pana metaṁ, sāriputta, sandhāya bhāsitaṁ pārāyane udayapañhe:
segs.e: And Sāriputta, this is what I was referring to in ‘The Way to the Far Shore’, in ‘The Questions of Udaya’ when I said:
‘The giving up of both
sensual desires and displeasures,
the casting aside of dullness,
and the prevention of remorse;
pure equanimity and mindfulness,
preceded by investigation of principles—
this, I declare, is liberation by enlightenment,
the smashing of ignorance.’”
Numbered Discourses 3.34
4. Messengers of the Gods
Sources
“Mendicants, there are these three sources that give rise to deeds.
What three?

segs.p: Lobho nidānaṁ kammānaṁ samudayāya, doso nidānaṁ kammānaṁ samudayāya, moho nidānaṁ kammānaṁ samudayāya.
segs.e: Greed, hate, and delusion are sources that give rise to deeds.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, lobhapakataṁ kammaṁ lobhajaṁ lobhanidānaṁ lobhasamudayaṁ, yatthassa attabhāvo nibbattati tattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati.
segs.e: Any deed that emerges from greed—born, sourced, and originated from greed—ripens where that new incarnation is born.

segs.p: Yattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati tattha tassa kammassa vipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedeti, diṭṭhe vā dhamme upapajja vā apare vā pariyāye.
segs.e: And wherever that deed ripens, its result is experienced—either in the present life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent period.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, dosapakataṁ kammaṁ dosajaṁ dosanidānaṁ dosasamudayaṁ, yatthassa attabhāvo nibbattati tattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati.
segs.e: Any deed that emerges from hate—born, sourced, and originated from hate—ripens where that new incarnation is born.

segs.p: Yattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati tattha tassa kammassa vipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedeti, diṭṭhe vā dhamme upapajja vā apare vā pariyāye.
segs.e: And wherever that deed ripens, its result is experienced—either in the present life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent period.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, mohapakataṁ kammaṁ mohajaṁ mohanidānaṁ mohasamudayaṁ, yatthassa attabhāvo nibbattati tattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati.
segs.e: Any deed that emerges from delusion—born, sourced, and originated from delusion—ripens where that new incarnation is born.

segs.p: Yattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati tattha tassa kammassa vipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedeti, diṭṭhe vā dhamme upapajja vā apare vā pariyāye.
segs.e: And wherever that deed ripens, its result is experienced—either in the present life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent period.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, bījāni akhaṇḍāni apūtīni avātātapahatāni sārādāni sukhasayitāni sukhette suparikammakatāya bhūmiyā nikkhittāni.
segs.e: Suppose some seeds were intact, unspoiled, not weather-damaged, fertile, and well-kept. They’re sown in a well-prepared, productive field,
and the heavens provide plenty of rain.

segs.p: Evassu tāni, bhikkhave, bījāni vuddhiṁ viruḷhiṁ vepullaṁ āpajjeyyuṁ.
segs.e: Then those seeds would grow, increase, and mature.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, yaṁ lobhapakataṁ kammaṁ lobhajaṁ lobhanidānaṁ lobhasamudayaṁ, yatthassa attabhāvo nibbattati tattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati.
segs.e: In the same way, any deed that emerges from greed—born, sourced, and originated from greed—ripens where that new incarnation is born.

segs.p: Yattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati tattha tassa kammassa vipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedeti, diṭṭhe vā dhamme upapajja vā apare vā pariyāye.
segs.e: And wherever that deed ripens, its result is experienced—either in the present life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent period.
Any deed that emerges from hate …

segs.p: yaṁ mohapakataṁ kammaṁ mohajaṁ mohanidānaṁ mohasamudayaṁ, yatthassa attabhāvo nibbattati tattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati.
segs.e: Any deed that emerges from delusion—born, sourced, and originated from delusion—ripens where that new incarnation is born.

segs.p: Yattha taṁ kammaṁ vipaccati tattha tassa kammassa vipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedeti, diṭṭhe vā dhamme upapajja vā apare vā pariyāye.
segs.e: And wherever that deed ripens, its result is experienced—either in the present life, or in the next life, or in some subsequent period.

segs.p: Imāni kho, bhikkhave, tīṇi nidānāni kammānaṁ samudayāya.
segs.e: These are three sources that give rise to deeds.
Mendicants, there are these three sources that give rise to deeds.
What three?

segs.p: Alobho nidānaṁ kammānaṁ samudayāya, adoso nidānaṁ kammānaṁ samudayāya, amoho nidānaṁ kammānaṁ samudayāya.
segs.e: Contentment, love, and understanding are sources that give rise to deeds.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, alobhapakataṁ kammaṁ alobhajaṁ alobhanidānaṁ alobhasamudayaṁ, lobhe vigate evaṁ taṁ kammaṁ pahīnaṁ hoti ucchinnamūlaṁ tālāvatthukataṁ anabhāvaṅkataṁ āyatiṁ anuppādadhammaṁ.
segs.e: Any deed that emerges from contentment—born, sourced, and originated from contentment—is given up when greed is done away with. It’s cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, adosapakataṁ kammaṁ adosajaṁ adosanidānaṁ adosasamudayaṁ, dose vigate evaṁ taṁ kammaṁ pahīnaṁ hoti ucchinnamūlaṁ tālāvatthukataṁ anabhāvaṅkataṁ āyatiṁ anuppādadhammaṁ.
segs.e: Any deed that emerges from love—born, sourced, and originated from love—is abandoned when hate is done away with. It’s cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, amohapakataṁ kammaṁ amohajaṁ amohanidānaṁ amohasamudayaṁ, mohe vigate evaṁ taṁ kammaṁ pahīnaṁ hoti ucchinnamūlaṁ tālāvatthukataṁ anabhāvaṅkataṁ āyatiṁ anuppādadhammaṁ.
segs.e: Any deed that emerges from understanding—born, sourced, and originated from understanding—is abandoned when delusion is done away with. It’s cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, bījāni akhaṇḍāni apūtīni avātātapahatāni sārādāni sukhasayitāni.
segs.e: Suppose some seeds were intact, unspoiled, not damaged by wind and sun, fertile, and well-kept.
But someone would burn them with fire,
reduce them to ashes,

segs.p: Masiṁ karitvā mahāvāte vā ophuṇeyya nadiyā vā sīghasotāya pavāheyya.
segs.e: and whisk away the ashes in a strong wind, or glide them down a swift stream.

segs.p: Evassu tāni, bhikkhave, bījāni ucchinnamūlāni tālāvatthukatāni anabhāvaṅkatāni āyatiṁ anuppādadhammāni.
segs.e: Then those seeds would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

segs.p: Evamevaṁ kho, bhikkhave, yaṁ alobhapakataṁ kammaṁ alobhajaṁ alobhanidānaṁ alobhasamudayaṁ, lobhe vigate evaṁ taṁ kammaṁ pahīnaṁ hoti ucchinnamūlaṁ tālāvatthukataṁ anabhāvaṅkataṁ āyatiṁ anuppādadhammaṁ.
segs.e: In the same way, any deed that emerges from contentment—born, sourced, and originated from contentment—is abandoned when greed is done away with. It’s cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.
Any deed that emerges from love …

segs.p: yaṁ amohapakataṁ kammaṁ amohajaṁ amohanidānaṁ amohasamudayaṁ, mohe vigate evaṁ taṁ kammaṁ pahīnaṁ hoti …pe…
segs.e: Any deed that emerges from understanding—born, sourced, and originated from understanding—is abandoned when delusion is done away with.
It’s cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.

segs.p: Imāni kho, bhikkhave, tīṇi nidānāni kammānaṁ samudayāyāti.
segs.e: These are three sources that give rise to deeds.
When an ignorant person acts
out of greed, hate, or delusion,
any deeds they have done,
a little or a lot,
are to be experienced right here,
not in any other place.
So a wise person,
a mendicant arousing knowledge
of the outcome of greed, hate, and delusion,
would abandon all bad destinies.”
Numbered Discourses 3.35
4. Messengers of the Gods
With Hatthaka
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā āḷaviyaṁ viharati gomagge siṁsapāvane paṇṇasanthare.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Āḷavī, on a mat of leaves by a cow-path in a rosewood grove.

segs.p: Atha kho hatthako āḷavako jaṅghāvihāraṁ anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramāno addasa bhagavantaṁ gomagge siṁsapāvane paṇṇasanthare nisinnaṁ.
segs.e: Then as Hatthaka of Āḷavī was going for a walk he saw the Buddha sitting on that mat of leaves.

segs.p: Disvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho hatthako āḷavako bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: He went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said,
“Sir, I trust the Buddha slept well?”
“Yes, prince, I slept well.

segs.p: Ye ca pana loke sukhaṁ senti, ahaṁ tesaṁ aññataro”ti.
segs.e: I am one of those who sleep at ease in the world.”

segs.p: “Sītā, bhante, hemantikā ratti, antaraṭṭhako himapātasamayo, kharā gokaṇṭakahatā bhūmi, tanuko paṇṇasantharo, viraḷāni rukkhassa pattāni, sītāni kāsāyāni vatthāni, sīto ca verambho vāto vāyati.
segs.e: “The winter nights are cold, sir, and it’s the week of mid-winter, when the snow falls. Rough is the ground trampled under the cows’ hooves, and thin is the mat of leaves. The leaves are sparse on the trees, the ocher robes are cold, and cold blows the north wind.
And yet the Buddha says,
‘Yes, prince, I slept well.

segs.p: Ye ca pana loke sukhaṁ senti, ahaṁ tesaṁ aññataro’”ti.
segs.e: I am one of those who sleep at ease in the world.’”

segs.p: “Tena hi, kumāra, taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi. Yathā te khameyya tathā naṁ byākareyyāsi.
segs.e: “Well then, prince, I’ll ask you about this in return, and you can answer as you like.

segs.p: Taṁ kiṁ maññasi, kumāra, idhassa gahapatissa vā gahapatiputtassa vā kūṭāgāraṁ ullittāvalittaṁ nivātaṁ phusitaggaḷaṁ pihitavātapānaṁ.
segs.e: What do you think? Take the case of a householder or his son, who lives in a bungalow, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with door fastened and window shuttered.

segs.p: Tatrassa pallaṅko gonakatthato paṭikatthato paṭalikatthato kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇo sauttaracchado ubhato lohitakūpadhāno;
segs.e: His couch is spread with woolen covers—shag-piled, pure white, or embroidered with flowers—and spread with a fine deer hide. It has a canopy above and red pillows at both ends.
An oil lamp is burning there,

segs.p: catasso ca pajāpatiyo manāpāmanāpena paccupaṭṭhitā assu.
segs.e: while his four wives attend to him in all manner of agreeable ways.

segs.p: Taṁ kiṁ maññasi, kumāra, sukhaṁ vā so sayeyya no vā?
segs.e: What do you think, prince, would he sleep at ease, or not?
Or how do you see this?”
“He would sleep at ease, sir.

segs.p: Ye ca pana loke sukhaṁ senti, so tesaṁ aññataro”ti.
segs.e: Of those who sleep at ease in the world, he would be one.”
“What do you think, prince?

segs.p: api nu tassa gahapatissa vā gahapatiputtassa vā uppajjeyyuṁ rāgajā pariḷāhā kāyikā vā cetasikā vā yehi so rāgajehi pariḷāhehi pariḍayhamāno dukkhaṁ sayeyyā”ti?
segs.e: Is it not possible that a fever born of greed—physical or mental—might arise in that householder or householder’s son, burning him so he sleeps badly?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Yehi kho so, kumāra, gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā rāgajehi pariḷāhehi pariḍayhamāno dukkhaṁ sayeyya, so rāgo tathāgatassa pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṅkato āyatiṁ anuppādadhammo.
segs.e: “The greed that burns that householder or householder’s son, making them sleep badly, has been cut off at the root by the Realized One, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.
That’s why I sleep at ease.
What do you think, prince?

segs.p: api nu tassa gahapatissa vā gahapatiputtassa vā uppajjeyyuṁ dosajā pariḷāhā …pe…
segs.e: Is it not possible that a fever born of hate …

segs.p: mohajā pariḷāhā kāyikā vā cetasikā vā yehi so mohajehi pariḷāhehi pariḍayhamāno dukkhaṁ sayeyyā”ti?
segs.e: or a fever born of delusion—physical or mental—might arise in that householder or householder’s son, burning him so he sleeps badly?”
“Yes, sir.”

segs.p: “Ye hi kho so, kumāra, gahapati vā gahapatiputto vā mohajehi pariḷāhehi pariḍayhamāno dukkhaṁ sayeyya, so moho tathāgatassa pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṅkato āyatiṁ anuppādadhammo.
segs.e: “The delusion that burns that householder or householder’s son, making them sleep badly, has been cut off at the root by the Realized One, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.
That’s why I sleep at ease.
A brahmin who is fully quenched
always sleeps at ease.
Sensual pleasures slip off them,
they’re cooled, free of attachments.
Since they’ve cut off all clinging,
and removed the stress from the heart,
the peaceful sleep at ease,
having found peace of mind.”
Numbered Discourses 3.36
4. Messengers of the Gods
Messengers of the Gods
“There are, mendicants, these three messengers of the gods.
What three?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco kāyena duccaritaṁ carati, vācāya duccaritaṁ carati, manasā duccaritaṁ carati.
segs.e: Firstly, someone does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: So kāyena duccaritaṁ caritvā, vācāya duccaritaṁ caritvā, manasā duccaritaṁ caritvā kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā nānābāhāsu gahetvā yamassa rañño dassenti:
segs.e: The wardens of hell take them by the arms and present them to King Yama, saying,

segs.p: ‘ayaṁ, deva, puriso amatteyyo apetteyyo asāmañño abrahmañño, na kule jeṭṭhāpacāyī.
segs.e: ‘Your Majesty, this person did not pay due respect to their mother and father, ascetics and brahmins, or honor the elders in the family.
May Your Majesty punish them!’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā paṭhamaṁ devadūtaṁ samanuyuñjati samanugāhati samanubhāsati:
segs.e: King Yama pursues, presses, and grills them about the first messenger of the gods:

segs.p: ‘ambho, purisa, na tvaṁ addasa manussesu paṭhamaṁ devadūtaṁ pātubhūtan’ti?
segs.e: ‘My man, did you not see the first messenger of the gods that appeared among human beings?’
They say,
‘I saw nothing, sir.’
King Yama says to them,

segs.p: ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṁ addasa manussesu itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā āsītikaṁ vā nāvutikaṁ vā vassasatikaṁ vā jātiyā jiṇṇaṁ gopānasivaṅkaṁ bhoggaṁ daṇḍaparāyaṇaṁ pavedhamānaṁ gacchantaṁ āturaṁ gatayobbanaṁ khaṇḍadantaṁ palitakesaṁ vilūnaṁ khallitasiraṁ valitaṁ tilakāhatagattan’ti?
segs.e: ‘My man, did you not see among human beings an elderly woman or a man—eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old—bent double, crooked, leaning on a staff, trembling as they walk, ailing, past their prime, with teeth broken, hair grey and scanty or bald, skin wrinkled, and limbs blotchy?’
They say,
‘I saw that, sir.’
King Yama says to them,

segs.p: ‘ambho, purisa, tassa te viññussa sato mahallakassa na etadahosi—
segs.e: ‘My man, did it not occur to you—being sensible and mature—

segs.p: ahampi khomhi jarādhammo jaraṁ anatīto, handāhaṁ kalyāṇaṁ karomi, kāyena vācāya manasā’ti?
segs.e: “I, too, am liable to grow old. I’m not exempt from old age. I’d better do good by way of body, speech, and mind”?’
They say,
‘I couldn’t, sir. I was negligent.’
King Yama says to them,

segs.p: ‘ambho, purisa, pamādatāya na kalyāṇamakāsi kāyena vācāya manasā.
segs.e: ‘My man, because you were negligent, you didn’t do good by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: Taggha tvaṁ, ambho purisa, tathā karissanti yathā taṁ pamattaṁ.
segs.e: Well, they’ll definitely punish you to fit your negligence.

segs.p: Taṁ kho pana te etaṁ pāpakammaṁ neva mātarā kataṁ, na pitarā kataṁ, na bhātarā kataṁ, na bhaginiyā kataṁ, na mittāmaccehi kataṁ, na ñātisālohitehi kataṁ, na devatāhi kataṁ, na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṁ;
segs.e: That bad deed wasn’t done by your mother, father, brother, or sister. It wasn’t done by friends and colleagues, by relatives and kin, by the deities, or by ascetics and brahmins.

segs.p: atha kho tayāvetaṁ pāpakammaṁ kataṁ, tvaññevetassa vipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedissasī’ti.
segs.e: That bad deed was done by you alone, and you alone will experience the result.’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā paṭhamaṁ devadūtaṁ samanuyuñjitvā samanugāhitvā samanubhāsitvā, dutiyaṁ devadūtaṁ samanuyuñjati samanugāhati samanubhāsati:
segs.e: King Yama grills them about the second messenger of the gods:

segs.p: ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṁ addasa manussesu dutiyaṁ devadūtaṁ pātubhūtan’ti?
segs.e: ‘My man, did you not see the second messenger of the gods that appeared among human beings?’
They say,
‘I saw nothing, sir.’
King Yama says to them,

segs.p: ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṁ addasa manussesu itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā ābādhikaṁ dukkhitaṁ bāḷhagilānaṁ, sake muttakarīse palipannaṁ semānaṁ, aññehi vuṭṭhāpiyamānaṁ, aññehi saṁvesiyamānan’ti?
segs.e: ‘My man, did you not see among human beings a woman or a man, sick, suffering, gravely ill, collapsed in their own urine and feces, being picked up by some and put down by others?’
They say,
‘I saw that, sir.’
King Yama says to them,

segs.p: ‘ambho purisa, tassa te viññussa sato mahallakassa na etadahosi:
segs.e: ‘My man, did it not occur to you—being sensible and mature—

segs.p: “ahampi khomhi byādhidhammo byādhiṁ anatīto, handāhaṁ kalyāṇaṁ karomi kāyena vācāya manasā”’ti?
segs.e: “I, too, am liable to become sick. I’m not exempt from sickness. I’d better do good by way of body, speech, and mind”?’
They say,
‘I couldn’t, sir. I was negligent.’
King Yama says to them,

segs.p: ‘ambho purisa, pamādatāya na kalyāṇamakāsi kāyena vācāya manasā.
segs.e: ‘My man, because you were negligent, you didn’t do good by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: Taggha tvaṁ, ambho purisa, tathā karissanti yathā taṁ pamattaṁ.
segs.e: Well, they’ll definitely punish you to fit your negligence.

segs.p: Taṁ kho pana te etaṁ pāpakammaṁ neva mātarā kataṁ, na pitarā kataṁ, na bhātarā kataṁ, na bhaginiyā kataṁ, na mittāmaccehi kataṁ, na ñātisālohitehi kataṁ, na devatāhi kataṁ, na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṁ;
segs.e: That bad deed wasn’t done by your mother, father, brother, or sister. It wasn’t done by friends and colleagues, by relatives and kin, by the deities, or by ascetics and brahmins.

segs.p: atha kho tayāvetaṁ pāpakammaṁ kataṁ. Tvaññevetassa vipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedissasī’ti.
segs.e: That bad deed was done by you alone, and you alone will experience the result.’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā dutiyaṁ devadūtaṁ samanuyuñjitvā samanugāhitvā samanubhāsitvā, tatiyaṁ devadūtaṁ samanuyuñjati samanugāhati samanubhāsati:
segs.e: King Yama grills them about the third messenger of the gods:

segs.p: ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṁ addasa manussesu tatiyaṁ devadūtaṁ pātubhūtan’ti?
segs.e: ‘My man, did you not see the third messenger of the gods that appeared among human beings?’
They say,
‘I saw nothing, sir.’
King Yama says to them,

segs.p: ‘ambho purisa, na tvaṁ addasa manussesu itthiṁ vā purisaṁ vā ekāhamataṁ vā dvīhamataṁ vā tīhamataṁ vā uddhumātakaṁ vinīlakaṁ vipubbakajātan’ti?
segs.e: ‘My man, did you not see among human beings a woman or a man, dead for one, two, or three days, bloated, livid, and festering?’
They say,
‘I saw that, sir.’
King Yama says to them,

segs.p: ‘ambho purisa, tassa te viññussa sato mahallakassa na etadahosi—
segs.e: ‘My man, did it not occur to you—being sensible and mature—

segs.p: ahampi khomhi maraṇadhammo maraṇaṁ anatīto, handāhaṁ kalyāṇaṁ karomi kāyena vācāya manasā’ti?
segs.e: “I, too, am liable to die. I’m not exempt from death. I’d better do good by way of body, speech, and mind”?’
They say,
‘I couldn’t, sir. I was negligent.’
King Yama says to them,

segs.p: ‘ambho purisa, pamādatāya na kalyāṇamakāsi kāyena vācāya manasā.
segs.e: ‘My man, because you were negligent, you didn’t do good by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: Taggha tvaṁ, ambho purisa, tathā karissanti yathā taṁ pamattaṁ.
segs.e: Well, they’ll definitely punish you to fit your negligence.

segs.p: Taṁ kho pana te etaṁ pāpakammaṁ neva mātarā kataṁ, na pitarā kataṁ, na bhātarā kataṁ, na bhaginiyā kataṁ, na mittāmaccehi kataṁ, na ñātisālohitehi kataṁ, na devatāhi kataṁ, na samaṇabrāhmaṇehi kataṁ;
segs.e: That bad deed wasn’t done by your mother, father, brother, or sister. It wasn’t done by friends and colleagues, by relatives and kin, by the deities, or by ascetics and brahmins.

segs.p: atha kho tayāvetaṁ pāpakammaṁ kataṁ. Tvaññevetassa vipākaṁ paṭisaṁvedissasī’”ti.
segs.e: That bad deed was done by you alone, and you alone will experience the result.’

segs.p: Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, yamo rājā tatiyaṁ devadūtaṁ samanuyuñjitvā samanugāhitvā samanubhāsitvā tuṇhī hoti.
segs.e: After grilling them about the third messenger of the gods, King Yama falls silent.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā pañcavidhabandhanaṁ nāma kāraṇaṁ karonti.
segs.e: The wardens of hell punish them with the five-fold crucifixion.

segs.p: Tattaṁ ayokhilaṁ hatthe gamenti. Tattaṁ ayokhilaṁ dutiyasmiṁ hatthe gamenti. Tattaṁ ayokhilaṁ pāde gamenti. Tattaṁ ayokhilaṁ dutiyasmiṁ pāde gamenti. Tattaṁ ayokhilaṁ majjhe urasmiṁ gamenti.
segs.e: They drive red-hot stakes through the hands and feet, and another in the middle of the chest.

segs.p: So tattha dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vediyati, na ca tāva kālaṁ karoti yāva na taṁ pāpakammaṁ byantīhoti.
segs.e: And there they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings—but they don’t die until that bad deed is eliminated.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā saṁvesetvā kudhārīhi tacchanti.
segs.e: The wardens of hell throw them down and hack them with axes. …

segs.p: So tattha dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vediyati, na ca tāva kālaṁ karoti yāva na taṁ pāpakammaṁ byantīhoti.
Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā uddhampādaṁ adhosiraṁ gahetvā vāsīhi tacchanti …pe…
segs.e: They hang them upside-down and hack them with hatchets. …

segs.p: tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā rathe yojetvā ādittāya bhūmiyā sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya sārentipi paccāsārentipi …pe…
segs.e: They harness them to a chariot, and drive them back and forth across burning ground, blazing and glowing. …

segs.p: tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā mahantaṁ aṅgārapabbataṁ ādittaṁ sampajjalitaṁ sajotibhūtaṁ āropentipi oropentipi …pe…
segs.e: They make them climb up and down a big mountain of burning coals, blazing and glowing. …

segs.p: tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, nirayapālā uddhampādaṁ adhosiraṁ gahetvā tattāya lohakumbhiyā pakkhipanti, ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya. (…)
segs.e: The wardens of hell turn them upside down and throw them in a red-hot copper pot, burning, blazing, and glowing.

segs.p: So tattha pheṇuddehakaṁ paccamāno sakimpi uddhaṁ gacchati, sakimpi adho gacchati, sakimpi tiriyaṁ gacchati.
segs.e: There they’re seared in boiling scum, and they’re swept up and down and round and round.

segs.p: So tattha dukkhā tibbā kharā kaṭukā vedanā vediyati, na ca tāva kālaṁ karoti yāva na taṁ pāpakammaṁ byantīhoti.
segs.e: And there they suffer painful, sharp, severe, acute feelings—but they don’t die until that bad deed is eliminated.
The wardens of hell toss them into the Great Hell.
Now, about that Great Hell:
‘Four are its corners, four its doors,
neatly divided section by section.
Surrounded by an iron wall,
of iron is its roof.
The ground is even made of iron,
it burns with fierce fire.
The heat forever radiates
a hundred leagues around.’
Once upon a time, King Yama thought,

segs.p: ‘ye kira, bho, loke pāpakāni kammāni karonti te evarūpā vividhā kammakāraṇā karīyanti.
segs.e: ‘Those who do such bad deeds in the world receive these many different punishments.

segs.p: Aho vatāhaṁ manussattaṁ labheyyaṁ, tathāgato ca loke uppajjeyya arahaṁ sammāsambuddho, tañcāhaṁ bhagavantaṁ payirupāseyyaṁ.
segs.e: Oh, I hope I may be reborn as a human being! And that a Realized One—a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha—arises in the world! And that I may pay homage to the Buddha!

segs.p: So ca me bhagavā dhammaṁ deseyya, tassa cāhaṁ bhagavato dhammaṁ ājāneyyan’ti.
segs.e: Let that Buddha teach me Dhamma, so that I may understand his teaching!’

segs.p: Taṁ kho panāhaṁ, bhikkhave, na aññassa samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā sutvā evaṁ vadāmi, api ca kho, bhikkhave, yadeva me sāmaṁ ñātaṁ sāmaṁ diṭṭhaṁ sāmaṁ viditaṁ tadevāhaṁ vadāmīti.
segs.e: Now, I don’t say this because I’ve heard it from some other ascetic or brahmin. I only say it because I’ve known, seen, and realized it for myself.
When warned by the gods’ messengers,
those sons of Manu who are negligent
sorrow for a long time
when they go to that wretched place.
When warned by the gods’ messengers,
the good and true persons here
never neglect
the teaching of the Noble One.
Seeing the danger in grasping,
the origin of birth and death,
the unattached are freed
with the ending of birth and death.
Happy, they’ve come to a safe place,
quenched in this very life.
They’ve gone beyond all enmities and fears,
and risen above all suffering.”
Numbered Discourses 3.37
4. Messengers of the Gods
The Four Great Kings (1st)

segs.p: “Aṭṭhamiyaṁ, bhikkhave, pakkhassa catunnaṁ mahārājānaṁ amaccā pārisajjā imaṁ lokaṁ anuvicaranti:
segs.e: “On the eighth day of the fortnight, mendicants, the ministers and councillors of the four great kings wander about the world, thinking:

segs.p: ‘kacci bahū manussā manussesu matteyyā petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino uposathaṁ upavasanti paṭijāgaronti puññāni karontī’ti.
segs.e: ‘Hopefully most humans are paying due respect to their parents, ascetics and brahmins, honoring the elders in their families, observing and keeping vigil on the sabbath, and making merit.’

segs.p: Cātuddasiṁ, bhikkhave, pakkhassa catunnaṁ mahārājānaṁ puttā imaṁ lokaṁ anuvicaranti:
segs.e: And on the fourteenth day of the fortnight, the sons of the four great kings wander about the world, thinking:

segs.p: ‘kacci bahū manussā manussesu matteyyā petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino uposathaṁ upavasanti paṭijāgaronti puññāni karontī’ti.
segs.e: ‘Hopefully most humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit.’

segs.p: Tadahu, bhikkhave, uposathe pannarase cattāro mahārājāno sāmaññeva imaṁ lokaṁ anuvicaranti:
segs.e: And on the fifteenth day sabbath, the four great kings themselves wander about the world, thinking:

segs.p: ‘kacci bahū manussā manussesu matteyyā petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino uposathaṁ upavasanti paṭijāgaronti puññāni karontī’ti.
segs.e: ‘Hopefully most humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit.’

segs.p: Sace, bhikkhave, appakā honti manussā manussesu matteyyā petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino uposathaṁ upavasanti paṭijāgaronti puññāni karonti.
segs.e: If only a few humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit,

segs.p: Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, cattāro mahārājāno devānaṁ tāvatiṁsānaṁ sudhammāya sabhāya sannisinnānaṁ sannipatitānaṁ ārocenti:
segs.e: the four great kings address the gods of the thirty-three, seated together in the Hall of Clear Right:

segs.p: ‘appakā kho, mārisā, manussā manussesu matteyyā petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino uposathaṁ upavasanti paṭijāgaronti puññāni karontī’ti.
segs.e: ‘Only a few humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit.’

segs.p: Tena kho, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṁsā anattamanā honti:
segs.e: Then the gods of the thirty-three are disappointed, thinking,

segs.p: ‘dibbā vata, bho, kāyā parihāyissanti, paripūrissanti asurakāyā’ti.
segs.e: ‘The heavenly hosts will dwindle, while the titan hosts will swell!’

segs.p: Sace pana, bhikkhave, bahū honti manussā manussesu matteyyā petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino uposathaṁ upavasanti paṭijāgaronti puññāni karonti.
segs.e: But if many humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit,

segs.p: Tamenaṁ, bhikkhave, cattāro mahārājāno devānaṁ tāvatiṁsānaṁ sudhammāya sabhāya sannisinnānaṁ sannipatitānaṁ ārocenti:
segs.e: the four great kings address the gods of the thirty-three, seated together in the Hall of Clear Right:

segs.p: ‘bahū kho, mārisā, manussā manussesu matteyyā petteyyā sāmaññā brahmaññā kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino uposathaṁ upavasanti paṭijāgaronti puññāni karontī’ti.
segs.e: ‘Many humans are paying due respect to their parents … and making merit.’

segs.p: Tena, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṁsā attamanā honti:
segs.e: Then the gods of the thirty-three are pleased, thinking,

segs.p: ‘dibbā vata bho kāyā paripūrissanti, parihāyissanti asurakāyā’ti.
segs.e: ‘The heavenly hosts will swell, while the titan hosts will dwindle!’

segs.p: Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo deve tāvatiṁse anunayamāno tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: Once upon a time, Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the thirty-three, spoke this verse:
‘Whoever wants to be like me
would observe the sabbath
complete in all eight factors,
on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,
and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as on the fortnightly special displays.’

segs.p: Sā kho panesā, bhikkhave, sakkena devānamindena gāthā duggītā na sugītā dubbhāsitā na subhāsitā.
segs.e: But that verse was poorly sung by Sakka, lord of gods, not well sung; poorly spoken, not well spoken.
Why is that?

segs.p: Sakko hi, bhikkhave, devānamindo avītarāgo avītadoso avītamoho.
segs.e: Because Sakka, lord of gods, is not free of greed, hate, and delusion.

segs.p: Yo ca kho so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṁ khīṇāsavo vusitavā brahmacariyo katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṁyojano sammadaññāvimutto, tassa kho etaṁ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno kallaṁ vacanāya:
segs.e: But for a mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—it is appropriate to say:
‘Whoever wants to be like me
would observe the sabbath,
complete in all eight factors,
on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,
and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as on the fortnightly special displays.’
Why is that?

segs.p: So hi, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vītarāgo vītadoso vītamoho”ti.
segs.e: Because that mendicant is free of greed, hate, and delusion.”
Numbered Discourses 3.38
4. Messengers of the Gods
The Four Great Kings (2nd)

segs.p: “Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, sakko devānamindo deve tāvatiṁse anunayamāno tāyaṁ velāyaṁ imaṁ gāthaṁ abhāsi:
segs.e: “Once upon a time, mendicants, Sakka, lord of gods, guiding the gods of the thirty-three, spoke this verse:
‘Whoever wants to be like me
would observe the sabbath
complete in all eight factors,
on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,
and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as on the fortnightly special displays.’

segs.p: Sā kho panesā, bhikkhave, sakkena devānamindena gāthā duggītā na sugītā dubbhāsitā na subhāsitā.
segs.e: But that verse was poorly sung by Sakka, lord of gods, not well sung; poorly spoken, not well spoken.
Why is that?

segs.p: Sakko hi, bhikkhave, devānamindo aparimutto jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, ‘aparimutto dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi.
segs.e: Because Sakka, lord of gods, is not exempt from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. He is not exempt from suffering, I say.

segs.p: Yo ca kho so, bhikkhave, bhikkhu arahaṁ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṁyojano sammadaññāvimutto, tassa kho etaṁ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno kallaṁ vacanāya:
segs.e: But for a mendicant who is perfected—with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their heart’s goal, utterly ended the fetter of continued existence, and is rightly freed through enlightenment—it is appropriate to say:
‘Whoever wants to be like me
would observe the sabbath,
complete in all eight factors,
on the fourteenth and the fifteenth days,
and the eighth day of the fortnight,
as well as on the fortnightly special displays.’
Why is that?

segs.p: So hi, bhikkhave, bhikkhu parimutto jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, ‘parimutto dukkhasmā’ti vadāmī”ti.
segs.e: Because that mendicant is exempt from rebirth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. He is exempt from suffering, I say.”
Numbered Discourses 3.39
4. Messengers of the Gods
A Delicate Lifestyle
“My lifestyle was delicate, mendicants, most delicate, extremely delicate.

segs.p: Mama sudaṁ, bhikkhave, pitu nivesane pokkharaṇiyo kāritā honti.
segs.e: In my father’s home, lotus ponds were made just for me.

segs.p: Ekattha sudaṁ, bhikkhave, uppalaṁ vappati, ekattha padumaṁ, ekattha puṇḍarīkaṁ, yāvadeva mamatthāya.
segs.e: In some, blue water lilies blossomed, while in others, there were pink or white lotuses, just for my benefit.

segs.p: Na kho panassāhaṁ, bhikkhave, akāsikaṁ candanaṁ dhāremi. Kāsikaṁ, bhikkhave, su me taṁ veṭhanaṁ hoti, kāsikā kañcukā, kāsikaṁ nivāsanaṁ, kāsiko uttarāsaṅgo.
segs.e: I only used sandalwood from Kāsi, and my turbans, jackets, sarongs, and upper robes also came from Kāsi.

segs.p: Rattindivaṁ kho pana me su taṁ, bhikkhave, setacchattaṁ dhārīyati:
segs.e: And a white parasol was held over me night and day, with the thought:

segs.p: ‘mā naṁ phusi sītaṁ vā uṇhaṁ vā tiṇaṁ vā rajo vā ussāvo vā’ti.
segs.e: ‘Don’t let cold, heat, grass, dust, or damp bother him.’

segs.p: Tassa mayhaṁ, bhikkhave, tayo pāsādā ahesuṁ—eko hemantiko, eko gimhiko, eko vassiko.
segs.e: I had three stilt longhouses—one for the winter, one for the summer, and one for the rainy season.

segs.p: So kho ahaṁ, bhikkhave, vassike pāsāde vassike cattāro māse nippurisehi tūriyehi paricārayamāno na heṭṭhāpāsādaṁ orohāmi.
segs.e: I stayed in a stilt longhouse without coming downstairs for the four months of the rainy season, where I was entertained by musicians—none of them men.

segs.p: Yathā kho pana, bhikkhave, aññesaṁ nivesane dāsakammakaraporisassa kaṇājakaṁ bhojanaṁ dīyati bilaṅgadutiyaṁ, evamevassu me, bhikkhave, pitu nivesane dāsakammakaraporisassa sālimaṁsodano dīyati.
segs.e: While the bondservants, workers, and staff in other houses are given sour gruel with false black pepper to eat, in my father’s home they are given fine rice with meat.

segs.p: Tassa mayhaṁ, bhikkhave, evarūpāya iddhiyā samannāgatassa evarūpena ca sukhumālena etadahosi:
segs.e: Amid such prosperity and such a delicate lifestyle, I thought:

segs.p: ‘assutavā kho puthujjano attanā jarādhammo samāno jaraṁ anatīto paraṁ jiṇṇaṁ disvā aṭṭīyati harāyati jigucchati attānaṁyeva atisitvā, ahampi khomhi jarādhammo jaraṁ anatīto.
segs.e: ‘When an unlearned ordinary person—who is liable to grow old, not being exempt from old age—sees someone else who is old, they’re horrified, repelled, and disgusted, overlooking the fact that they themselves are in the same situation.

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana jarādhammo samāno jaraṁ anatīto paraṁ jiṇṇaṁ disvā aṭṭīyeyyaṁ harāyeyyaṁ jiguccheyyaṁ na metaṁ assa patirūpan’ti.
segs.e: But since I, too, am liable to grow old, it would not be appropriate for me to be horrified, embarrassed, and disgusted, when I see someone else who is old.’

segs.p: Tassa mayhaṁ, bhikkhave, iti paṭisañcikkhato yo yobbane yobbanamado so sabbaso pahīyi.
segs.e: Reflecting like this, I entirely gave up the vanity of youth.

segs.p: Assutavā kho puthujjano attanā byādhidhammo samāno byādhiṁ anatīto paraṁ byādhitaṁ disvā aṭṭīyati harāyati jigucchati attānaṁyeva atisitvā:
segs.e: ‘When an unlearned ordinary person—who is liable to get sick, not being exempt from sickness—sees someone else who is sick, they’re horrified, repelled, and disgusted, overlooking the fact that they themselves are in the same situation.

segs.p: ‘ahampi khomhi byādhidhammo byādhiṁ anatīto, ahañceva kho pana byādhidhammo samāno byādhiṁ anatīto paraṁ byādhikaṁ disvā aṭṭīyeyyaṁ harāyeyyaṁ jiguccheyyaṁ, na metaṁ assa patirūpan’ti.
segs.e: But since I, too, am liable to get sick, it would not be appropriate for me to be horrified, embarrassed, and disgusted, when I see someone else who is sick.’

segs.p: Tassa mayhaṁ, bhikkhave, iti paṭisañcikkhato yo ārogye ārogyamado so sabbaso pahīyi.
segs.e: Reflecting like this, I entirely gave up the vanity of health.

segs.p: Assutavā kho puthujjano attanā maraṇadhammo samāno maraṇaṁ anatīto paraṁ mataṁ disvā aṭṭīyati harāyati jigucchati attānaṁyeva atisitvā:
segs.e: ‘When an unlearned ordinary person—who is liable to die, not being exempt from death—sees someone else who is dead, they’re horrified, repelled, and disgusted, overlooking the fact that they themselves are in the same situation.

segs.p: ‘ahampi khomhi maraṇadhammo, maraṇaṁ anatīto, ahaṁ ceva kho pana maraṇadhammo samāno maraṇaṁ anatīto paraṁ mataṁ disvā aṭṭīyeyyaṁ harāyeyyaṁ jiguccheyyaṁ, na metaṁ assa patirūpan’ti.
segs.e: But since I, too, am liable to die, it would not be appropriate for me to be horrified, embarrassed, and disgusted, when I see someone else who is dead.’

segs.p: Tassa mayhaṁ, bhikkhave, iti paṭisañcikkhato yo jīvite jīvitamado so sabbaso pahīyīti.
segs.e: Reflecting like this, I entirely gave up the vanity of life.
There are these three vanities.
What three?
The vanity of youth, of health, and of life.

segs.p: Yobbanamadamatto vā, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano kāyena duccaritaṁ carati, vācāya duccaritaṁ carati, manasā duccaritaṁ carati.
segs.e: Intoxicated with the vanity of youth, an unlearned ordinary person does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: So kāyena duccaritaṁ caritvā, vācāya duccaritaṁ caritvā, manasā duccaritaṁ caritvā kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.
Intoxicated with the vanity of health …

segs.p: jīvitamadamatto vā, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano kāyena duccaritaṁ carati, vācāya duccaritaṁ carati, manasā duccaritaṁ carati.
segs.e: Intoxicated with the vanity of life, an unlearned ordinary person does bad things by way of body, speech, and mind.

segs.p: So kāyena duccaritaṁ caritvā, vācāya duccaritaṁ caritvā, manasā duccaritaṁ caritvā kāyassa bhedā paraṁ maraṇā apāyaṁ duggatiṁ vinipātaṁ nirayaṁ upapajjati.
segs.e: When their body breaks up, after death, they’re reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell.

segs.p: Yobbanamadamatto vā, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sikkhaṁ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattati.
segs.e: Intoxicated with the vanity of youth, health, or life, a mendicant resigns the training and returns to a lesser life.

segs.p: jīvitamadamatto vā, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sikkhaṁ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattatīti.

segs.e: For others, sickness is natural,
and so are old age and death.
Though this is how their nature is,
ordinary people feel disgusted.
If I were to be disgusted
with creatures whose nature is such,
it would not be appropriate for me,
since my life is just the same.
Living in such a way,
I understood the truth without attachments.
I mastered all vanities—
of health, of youth,
and even of life—
seeing renunciation as sanctuary.
Zeal sprang up in me
as I looked to extinguishment.
Now I’m unable
to indulge in sensual pleasures;
there’s no turning back,
I’m committed to the spiritual life.”
Numbered Discourses 3.40
4. Messengers from the Gods
In Charge
“There are, mendicants, these three things to put in charge.
What three?
Putting oneself, the world, or the teaching in charge.
And what, mendicants, is putting oneself in charge?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā iti paṭisañcikkhati:
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

segs.p: ‘na kho panāhaṁ cīvarahetu agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito.
segs.e: ‘I didn’t go forth from the lay life to homelessness for the sake of a robe,

segs.p: Na piṇḍapātahetu, na senāsanahetu, na itibhavābhavahetu agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito.
segs.e: almsfood, lodgings, or rebirth in this or that state.

segs.p: Api ca khomhi otiṇṇo jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto.
segs.e: But I was swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I was swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

segs.p: Appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethāti.
segs.e: And I thought, “Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.”

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana yādisake kāme ohāya agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito tādisake vā kāme pariyeseyyaṁ tato vā pāpiṭṭhatare, na metaṁ patirūpan’ti.
segs.e: But it would not be appropriate for me to seek sensual pleasures like those I abandoned when I went forth, or even worse.’
Then they reflect:

segs.p: ‘āraddhaṁ kho pana me vīriyaṁ bhavissati asallīnaṁ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṁ cittaṁ ekaggan’ti.
segs.e: ‘My energy shall be roused up and unflagging, mindfulness shall be established and lucid, my body shall be tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind shall be immersed in samādhi.’

segs.p: So attānaṁyeva adhipatiṁ karitvā akusalaṁ pajahati, kusalaṁ bhāveti, sāvajjaṁ pajahati, anavajjaṁ bhāveti, suddhaṁ attānaṁ pariharati.
segs.e: Putting themselves in charge, they give up the unskillful and develop the skillful, they give up the blameworthy and develop the blameless, and they keep themselves pure.
This is called putting oneself in charge.
And what, mendicants, is putting the world in charge?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā iti paṭisañcikkhati:
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

segs.p: ‘na kho panāhaṁ cīvarahetu agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito.
segs.e: ‘I didn’t go forth from the lay life to homelessness for the sake of a robe,

segs.p: Na piṇḍapātahetu, na senāsanahetu, na itibhavābhavahetu agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito.
segs.e: almsfood, lodgings, or rebirth in this or that state.

segs.p: Api ca khomhi otiṇṇo jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto.
segs.e: But I was swamped by rebirth, old age, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I was swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

segs.p: Appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethā’ti.
segs.e: And I thought, “Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.”

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana evaṁ pabbajito samāno kāmavitakkaṁ vā vitakkeyyaṁ, byāpādavitakkaṁ vā vitakkeyyaṁ, vihiṁsāvitakkaṁ vā vitakkeyyaṁ, mahā kho panāyaṁ lokasannivāso.
segs.e: And now, since I’ve now gone forth, I might have sensual, malicious, or cruel thoughts. But the population of the world is large,

segs.p: Mahantasmiṁ kho pana lokasannivāse santi samaṇabrāhmaṇā iddhimanto dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduno.
segs.e: and there are ascetics and brahmins who have psychic power—they’re clairvoyant, and can read the minds of others.

segs.p: Te dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṁ pajānanti.
segs.e: They see far without being seen, even by those close; and they understand the minds of others.
They would know me:

segs.p: ‘passatha, bho, imaṁ kulaputtaṁ saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti.
segs.e: “Look at this gentleman; he’s gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, but he’s living mixed up with bad, unskillful qualities.”

segs.p: devatāpi kho santi iddhimantiniyo dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduniyo.
segs.e: And there are deities, too, who have psychic power—they’re clairvoyant, and can read the minds of others.

segs.p: Tā dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṁ jānanti.
segs.e: They see far without being seen, even by those close; and they understand the minds of others.
They would know me:

segs.p: ‘passatha, bho, imaṁ kulaputtaṁ saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti.
segs.e: “Look at this gentleman; he’s gone forth out of faith from the lay life to homelessness, but he’s living mixed up with bad, unskillful qualities.”’
Then they reflect:

segs.p: ‘āraddhaṁ kho pana me vīriyaṁ bhavissati asallīnaṁ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṁ cittaṁ ekaggan’ti.
segs.e: ‘My energy shall be roused up and unflagging, mindfulness shall be established and lucid, my body shall be tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind shall be immersed in samādhi.’

segs.p: So lokaṁyeva adhipatiṁ karitvā akusalaṁ pajahati, kusalaṁ bhāveti, sāvajjaṁ pajahati, anavajjaṁ bhāveti, suddhaṁ attānaṁ pariharati.
segs.e: Putting the world in charge, they give up the unskillful and develop the skillful, they give up the blameworthy and develop the blameless, and they keep themselves pure.
This is called putting the world in charge.
And what, mendicants, is putting the teaching in charge?

segs.p: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato vā suññāgāragato vā iti paṭisañcikkhati:
segs.e: It’s when a mendicant has gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, and reflects like this:

segs.p: ‘na kho panāhaṁ cīvarahetu agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito.
segs.e: ‘I didn’t go forth from the lay life to homelessness for the sake of a robe,

segs.p: Na piṇḍapātahetu, na senāsanahetu, na itibhavābhavahetu agārasmā anagāriyaṁ pabbajito.
segs.e: almsfood, lodgings, or rebirth in this or that state.

segs.p: Api ca khomhi otiṇṇo jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, dukkhotiṇṇo dukkhapareto.
segs.e: But I was swamped by rebirth, old age, and death, by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I was swamped by suffering, mired in suffering.

segs.p: Appeva nāma imassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa antakiriyā paññāyethāti.
segs.e: And I thought, “Hopefully I can make an end to this entire mass of suffering.”

segs.p: Svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo sandiṭṭhiko akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṁ veditabbo viññūhīti.
segs.e: The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—apparent in the present life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.

segs.p: Santi kho pana me sabrahmacārī jānaṁ passaṁ viharanti.
segs.e: I have spiritual companions who live knowing and seeing.

segs.p: Ahañceva kho pana evaṁ svākkhāte dhammavinaye pabbajito samāno kusīto vihareyyaṁ pamatto, na metaṁ assa patirūpan’ti.
segs.e: Now that I’ve gone forth in this well explained teaching and training, it would not be appropriate for me to live lazy and heedless.’
Then they reflect:

segs.p: ‘āraddhaṁ kho pana me vīriyaṁ bhavissati asallīnaṁ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṁ cittaṁ ekaggan’ti.
segs.e: ‘My energy shall be roused up and unflagging, mindfulness shall be established and lucid, my body shall be tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind shall be immersed in samādhi.’

segs.p: So dhammaṁyeva adhipatiṁ karitvā akusalaṁ pajahati, kusalaṁ bhāveti, sāvajjaṁ pajahati, anavajjaṁ bhāveti, suddhaṁ attānaṁ pariharati.
segs.e: Putting the teaching in charge, they give up the unskillful and develop the skillful, they give up the blameworthy and develop the blameless, and they keep themselves pure.
This is called putting the teaching in charge.
These are the three things to put in charge.
There’s no privacy in the world,
for someone who does bad deeds.
You’ll know for yourself,
whether you’ve lied or told the truth.
When you witness your good self,
you despise it;
while you disguise
your bad self inside yourself.
The gods and the Realized One see
the fool who lives unjustly in the world.
So with yourself in charge, live mindfully;
with the world in charge, <j>be alert and practice absorption;
with the teaching in charge, <j>live in line with that teaching:
a sage who tries for the truth doesn’t deteriorate.
Māra’s conquered; the terminator’s overcome:
one who strives reaches the end of rebirth.
Unaffected, intelligent, knowing the world—
that sage is determined by nothing at all.”
Numbered Discourses 3.41
5. The Lesser Chapter
Present

segs.p: “Tiṇṇaṁ, bhikkhave, sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṁ puññaṁ pasavati.
segs.e: “Mendicants, when three things are present, a faithful gentleman brims with much merit.
What three?

segs.p: Saddhāya, bhikkhave, sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṁ puññaṁ pasavati.
segs.e: When faith is present,

segs.p: Deyyadhammassa, bhikkhave, sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṁ puññaṁ pasavati.
segs.e: when a gift to give is present,

segs.p: Dakkhiṇeyyānaṁ, bhikkhave, sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṁ puññaṁ pasavati.
segs.e: and when those worthy of a religious donation are present.

segs.p: Imesaṁ kho, bhikkhave, tiṇṇaṁ sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṁ puññaṁ pasavatī”ti.
segs.e: When these three things are present, a faithful gentleman brims with much merit.”
Numbered Discourses 3.42
5. The Lesser Chapter
Three Grounds
“There are three grounds, mendicants, by which a person with faith and confidence can be known.
What three?

segs.p: Sīlavantānaṁ dassanakāmo hoti, saddhammaṁ sotukāmo hoti, vigatamalamaccherena cetasā agāraṁ ajjhāvasati muttacāgo payatapāṇi vossaggarato yācayogo dānasaṁvibhāgarato.
segs.e: They like to see ethical people. They like to hear the true teaching. And they live at home with heart rid of the stain of stinginess, freely generous, open-handed, loving to let go, committed to charity, loving to give and to share.

segs.p: Imehi kho, bhikkhave, tīhi ṭhānehi saddho pasanno veditabbo.
segs.e: These are the three grounds by which a person with faith and confidence can be known.
They like to see ethical people;
they want to hear the true teaching;
they’ve driven out the stain of stinginess:
that’s who’s called an individual of faith.”
Numbered Discourses 3.43
5. The Lesser Chapter
Good Reasons

segs.p: “Tayo, bhikkhave, atthavase sampassamānena alameva paresaṁ dhammaṁ desetuṁ.
segs.e: “Mendicants, taking three reasons into consideration provides quite enough motivation to teach Dhamma to another.
What three?

segs.p: Yo dhammaṁ deseti so atthappaṭisaṁvedī ca hoti dhammappaṭisaṁvedī ca.
segs.e: When the teacher understands the meaning and the teaching.

segs.p: Yo dhammaṁ suṇāti so atthappaṭisaṁvedī ca hoti dhammappaṭisaṁvedī ca.
segs.e: When the audience understands the meaning and the teaching.

segs.p: Yo ceva dhammaṁ deseti yo ca dhammaṁ suṇāti ubho atthappaṭisaṁvedino ca honti dhammappaṭisaṁvedino ca.
segs.e: When both the teacher and the audience understand the meaning and the teaching.

segs.p: Ime kho, bhikkhave, tayo atthavase sampassamānena alameva paresaṁ dhammaṁ desetun”ti.
segs.e: Taking these three reasons into consideration provides quite enough motivation to teach Dhamma to another.”
Numbered Discourses 3.44
5. The Lesser Chapter
When Conversation Flows
“In three situations, mendicants, conversation flows.
What three?
